deck: CS3357A Networks::Quiz 1 Review::True or false traps

fields.Front: True or false: propagation delay depends on packet length and link rate.
fields.Back: False. dprop = d/s depends only on distance and medium. dtrans = L/R is the one that depends on L and R.

fields.Front: True or false: transmission delay grows with the length of the link.
fields.Back: False. dtrans = L/R has nothing to do with distance.

fields.Front: True or false: in cable (HFC) access, each home has a dedicated line to the CMTS.
fields.Back: False. Homes share the access network to the cable headend. A dedicated line is DSL (to the DSLAM).

fields.Front: True or false: DSL is a shared access technology.
fields.Back: False. DSL uses a dedicated telephone line to the central office.

fields.Front: True or false: forwarding determines the source-to-destination path a packet takes.
fields.Back: False. That is routing (global). Forwarding is local: input link → output link using the forwarding table.

fields.Front: True or false: in TDM each call transmits at the max rate of its own narrow frequency band.
fields.Back: False. That is FDM. In TDM each call uses the max rate of the wider band, but only during its time slots.

fields.Front: True or false: in circuit switching, an idle circuit segment can be used by other calls.
fields.Back: False. The circuit segment sits idle if not used by its call: no sharing.

fields.Front: True or false: a router begins transmitting a packet on the next link as soon as the first bits arrive.
fields.Back: False. Store-and-forward: the entire packet must arrive at the router first.

fields.Front: True or false: when La/R > 1, the average queueing delay is large but finite.
fields.Back: False. More work arrives than can be serviced, so the average delay is infinite. "Large" is the La/R → 1 case.

fields.Front: True or false: a packet dropped at a full buffer is always retransmitted by the source.
fields.Back: False. It may be retransmitted by the previous node, by the source end system, or not at all.

fields.Front: True or false: end-to-end throughput = max(R<sub>s</sub>, R<sub>c</sub>).
fields.Back: False. It is the min: the bottleneck link's rate.

fields.Front: True or false: wireless radio is full-duplex.
fields.Back: False. The slides call it broadcast and half-duplex (sender to receiver).

fields.Front: True or false: Google is a tier-1 ISP.
fields.Back: False. Google is a content provider network, a private network that often bypasses tier-1 and regional ISPs. The tier-1 examples are Level 3, Sprint, AT&T, NTT.

fields.Front: True or false: a router implements all five layers of the Internet stack.
fields.Back: False. A router implements network, link, physical (3). A switch implements link, physical (2). Hosts implement all five.

fields.Front: True or false: coaxial cable and radio are both guided media.
fields.Back: False. Coax is guided (solid medium). Radio is unguided (propagates freely).

fields.Front: True or false: "RFC" stands for Request for Change, and RFCs come from the IEEE.
fields.Back: False. RFC = Request for Comments, published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force).

fields.Front: True or false: the transport layer routes datagrams from source to destination.
fields.Back: False. That is the network layer (IP). Transport = process-to-process data transfer (TCP, UDP).

fields.Front: True or false: a protocol defines only the format of the messages exchanged.
fields.Back: False. A protocol defines format, order of messages sent and received, and actions taken on transmission and receipt.

fields.Front: True or false: in packet switching, each packet is sent at a fraction of the link's capacity.
fields.Back: False. Each packet is transmitted at full link capacity (slide 39).

fields.Front: True or false: connecting every access ISP directly to every other scales as O(N).
fields.Back: False. O(N2) connections, which is why it doesn't scale (slide 49).
